title: Grammatical Renunciation
paragraphs: It was a mutt looking like a palace, adorned with a front hall that resembled Hari engrossed in deep sleep over the mythical athiseshan snake. A young ascetic was sitting on the veranda of that mutt looking forward to the arrival of somebody.
Not just that. His ears were keenly expecting the unlocking sound from the adjacent prayer room, while the eyes kept a vigil on the door of the room.

The door did not open. But then the Tamil teacher, teaching literature to the chief priest of the mutt, appeared well before the expected time. With the sacred Vaishnavite religious mark on his forehead and a book in his hand, the teacher came near the young monk.
“What Ciṉṉaccāmi (junior monk), how are you?” asked the teacher.
“Teacher, sir! I am the junior pontiff of this mutt. You are referring to me as if I were Kiḷappāḷuvūr Ciṉṉaccāmi who self-immolated.”
“Pardon me. He was but a lion-hearted Tamil.”
“Since I am keeping guard here, am I then an ugly Tamilian?”
“Okay, leave it. The nocturnal chic would have come. Have they fled off?”
“You, teacher! How come you ask of such things without any inhibition?”
“Why should I be afraid? Are the pontiffs devoted to God in deep sleep after exhaustion, or are they taking a rest? Is this an unbroken meditation? That is what I am asking.”
“That does not allow you to raise questions breaking the rules of grammar!”
“It is a long time since some monks have forgotten and abandoned the norms of ascetic life. Well then, junior monk! Pray, which grammatical rule have I broken?”

“You used the plural verb while referring to one nocturnal chic, and in the same vein you referred to the single pontiff in the room using a plural suffix. According to your statement, how many pontiffs are there in the room? How many nocturnal chics? One pontiff and many nocturnal chics? Or, one nocturnal chic and many pontiffs?”

“Junior pontiff, don’t be confused! My question was based on a sound grammatical principle. The plural suffix is used for referring to a single man or woman. Singulars being referred to by plural suffixes are used as honorifics. It is indeed based on established grammatical rules which Tolkāppiyar calls admissible deviations.”

“Is that so!” exclaimed the junior monk with a gaping mouth, just as the door of the room opened. The colourful damsel released from the bedroom staggered her way out through the backdoor of the mutt. The teacher caught hold of the junior monk and recited the relevant verse from Tolkāppiyam:

> Plural suffix to a noun denoting human species singular > And plural suffix to a noun denoting non-human species singular > Are part of worldly usage in honour clothed, > Not permitted they are by norms of grammar though. > > (Collatikāram : Kiḷaviyākkam, verse 27)
